title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: An Overview
text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pairs a language model with a search index so that relevant passages are fetched at question time and placed in the prompt. Because the knowledge lives in the index rather than in the model weights, a RAG system can be updated by re-indexing documents without retraining anything. Retrieved passages give the answer a concrete source, which makes it easier to attribute claims and audit mistakes. RAG keeps each prompt small because only the most relevant chunks are sent to the model, which keeps per-question cost low even when the document collection is very large.

title: Where Retrieval Pipelines Fail
text: A RAG answer is only as good as its retrieval step: if the relevant passage is not retrieved, the model cannot use it and may answer from memory instead. Chunking choices matter, because splitting a document at the wrong place can separate a claim from the context needed to interpret it. Questions that require combining information scattered across many documents are hard for retrieval pipelines, since top-k search returns a handful of passages rather than the whole picture. Teams therefore need to evaluate retrieval quality separately from answer quality.

title: What Long-Context Models Can Do
text: Long-context models accept hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single prompt, which lets an entire contract, codebase or report be placed in front of the model at once. With the full document in view there is no retrieval step that can miss a relevant passage, so questions that span many sections can be answered in a single pass. Long context also simplifies the system, because there is no index to build, chunk or keep fresh. The approach works best when the relevant material is a single bounded corpus that fits inside the window.

title: The Limits of Very Long Prompts
text: Accuracy of long-context models is not uniform across the window: several studies report that information placed in the middle of a long prompt is used less reliably than information at the start or end. Simple needle-in-a-haystack tests can overstate real performance, because realistic questions require reasoning over many details rather than retrieving one planted sentence. A collection larger than the context window cannot be used at all without some form of selection or summarisation. Filling the window with irrelevant text can also distract the model and reduce answer quality.

title: Cost and Latency of RAG versus Long Context
text: Every token placed in a prompt is billed and processed, so sending a very large document with every question makes long-context answers slower and more expensive than answers built from a few retrieved passages. Prompt caching can reduce the cost of repeatedly sending the same long document, but it only helps when many questions share an identical prefix. RAG adds the latency of a search step, although that step is usually small compared with processing a very long prompt. Cost therefore tends to favour retrieval for large collections that are queried often.

title: Practical Guidance: Combining Retrieval and Long Context
text: A common hybrid design uses retrieval to narrow a large collection down to a few relevant documents and then places those whole documents in a long-context prompt. This reduces the risk of chunking away important context while keeping the prompt far smaller than the full collection. For a single bounded document, simply using long context is often the simplest choice. Teams should benchmark both approaches on their own questions, since the best choice depends on collection size, query volume and how much reasoning across documents is required.
